content: Efforts must be intensified to support research on snakebite envenoming and to develop targeted solutions for specific challenges. This includes modernizing and improving current antivenom production technologies and products. The World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with its partners, will establish a comprehensive framework for planning, monitoring, and evaluating the progress of the strategy over time. This framework will be integrated into national plans in countries where snakebite envenoming is a significant public health issue. Progress toward these objectives will be regularly assessed, with annual reports made publicly available. For each of the four strategic objectives, pathways for short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes will be prioritized. The tasks undertaken will yield both independent and interconnected results, which will synergistically strengthen each other and contribute to achieving the 12-year target. While the pathways to these objectives may not follow a linear progression, they will complement and support the overarching goals, such as improved antivenom products, better-trained healthcare workers, and adequately resourced health facilities to manage snakebite envenoming. Community engagement will also promote greater use of allopathic health services and antivenom treatments, increasing demand for antivenom and reversing the current vicious cycle that has led to a crisis in antivenom supply in sub-Saharan Africa and other regions. The planning, monitoring, and evaluation framework will be developed during the initial phase of the strategy and updated throughout the program. As baseline data and progress data improve, the framework will evolve to include both general elements and context-specific components. WHO will prepare outcome-based work plans for implementing the strategy's phases. Interventions will be planned within context-specific frameworks, using a SMART approach (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) to achieve short-, mid-, and long-term outcomes. Each component will be integrated into a risk mitigation matrix, with actions taken to manage risks effectively. Timelines, budgets, and deliverables will be mapped, and resources will be identified and secured. Planning will be updated annually or as needed. A monitoring framework will be developed with indicators for each outcome to track progress using various data sources and verification methods. Reports and data will be collected and aggregated regularly to monitor overall and context-specific progress. WHO will evaluate progress toward objectives and outcome targets, with a focus on relevant indicators of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 and WHO’s Thirteenth General Programme of Work (2019–2023) and subsequent programs. Evaluations will be conducted at the end of each strategy phase to assess progress and achievements at national, regional, and global levels. WHO will also create an adaptable template for the theory of change to enhance strategy implementation by aligning context and assumptions with a logical model for mapping steps, actions, or milestones for short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes. WHO will collaborate with countries and partners to define baseline data requirements and establish processes for acquiring and analyzing information. WHO will employ a robust risk mitigation model to identify, assess, and address risks that could impact the strategy's implementation. External risks will be managed using validated risk assessment tools to identify and mitigate potential threats early. Risk management will be pragmatic and strategic, with regular progress reviews and expert consultations to address emerging challenges effectively. The budget for the strategy will be incremental, with annual costs increasing as the strategy expands to include more countries. A significant portion of the budget will be allocated to country-level activities, with additional funding for regional coordination and collaboration. Prevention and control of snakebite envenoming will be integrated into broader national and sub-national health plans to maximize impact and reduce duplication. During the pilot phase (2019–2020), efforts will focus on strengthening communities and health systems in 10–12 countries where snakebite envenoming is a public health problem. Funding will also support the assessment of antivenom safety and effectiveness, the establishment of a trial antivenom stockpile for sub-Saharan Africa, and improvements in antivenom manufacturing, innovation, and modernization. Monitoring and evaluation of activities will provide the data necessary for effective planning and review, ensuring that the strategy remains adaptable to economic and other changes over time. The ultimate goal is to reduce deaths and disabilities from snakebite envenoming by 50% by 2030, ensuring better care for all patients and advancing progress toward the SDGs and universal health coverage.
